t: 3538. Merge Operations for Minimum Travel Time
o: Exactly k merges remove k interior signs; each removed sign's time adds to the next surviving sign. If surviving signs are p₀=0 < p₁ < … < p_m = n−1, the segment between consecutive survivors p and q travels at rate time[p] + … + time[q−1] (all merged rates pile onto the later sign). With n ≤ 50 and k ≤ 10, an O(n²k) interval DP is instant: dp[i][j] = minimal time reaching sign i (kept) using j merges among the first i signs.
k: Between two kept signs p and i, the travel rate is the summed time over all original segments in between — a prefix-sum lookup.
Removing the signs strictly between p and i costs exactly i−p−1 merges, linking the DP indices directly.
Answer is dp[n−1][k]; sign n−1 (the endpoint) is always kept.

a.n: Approach 1: Interval DP over kept signs
a.i: dp[i][j] = min travel time from position 0 to position[i] where sign i is kept and j merges have been spent among signs 0..i. Transition: choose the previous kept sign p; the gap removes i−p−1 signs (so j−(i−p−1) merges were used before), and the segment costs (position[i]−position[p]) × (timeSum(p..i−1)).
s: Prefix sums T of time so any segment rate is T[i] − T[p].
dp[0][0] = 0; fill i ascending, j from 0..min(k, i−1).
For each i, j, try every previous kept sign p < i with j−(i−p−1) ≥ 0 and relax dp[i][j].
a.t: O(n²·k) — at most 50·50·11 states with linear transitions

w: The modeling insight is that a merge's effect is entirely captured by 'rate sums onto the next kept sign', turning arbitrary merge sequences into choosing which signs survive. Verify with example 1: keeping signs 0,2,3 gives segment 0→2 rate 5 (40 min) and 2→3 rate 8+3=11 (22 min) = 62. Pitfalls: allowing merges at index 0 or n−1 (the constraints forbid removing the endpoints — encoded by requiring i−p−1 interior signs), and miscounting merges as i−p instead of i−p−1. Edge cases: k = 0 (answer is the untouched travel time), k = n−2 (collapse to two signs). Follow-up: return the merge sequence, or allow at most k merges.
